hook: Two thousand years ago a man wrote his friend a letter that just said: I'm not ill, and I'm not well.
story: His name was Serenus. He wasn't in crisis. Nothing had collapsed. He just couldn't tell if anything was wrong. So he wrote to Seneca and tried to describe it: I am neither sick nor well. Then this: I am distressed, not by a tempest, but by sea-sickness. No storm. Just the sway.
lesson: If you've been flat for weeks and can't point at a reason, that's it. It has a name and it's old. Seneca didn't tell him to toughen up. He wrote him a whole book back. Tonight, do the Serenus thing. Text one person the actual sentence: I'm not bad, I'm just off.
quote: I am neither sick nor well.
author: Serenus, quoted by Seneca
citation: De Tranquillitate Animi I, trans. Aubrey Stewart
tonight: Text one person: "I'm not bad, I'm just off."
broll: a man lying awake in a dark bedroom
a phone screen glowing at night
calm open sea from a boat deck
a hand holding a phone, unsent message

hook: Marcus Aurelius broke down crying in public when his teacher died, and the palace staff moved in to stop him.
story: Marcus was young. His tutor died and he wept where people could see it, and the court officials closed in to shut it down. Then the emperor, his adoptive father, stopped them with one sentence: Let him be only a man for once; for neither philosophy nor empire takes away natural feeling.
lesson: That is the head of the Roman Empire telling a room full of men to leave a crying boy alone. Two thousand years of people using Stoicism to mean don't feel it, and it starts with an emperor saying the opposite. You're allowed. Tonight, if something's sitting in your throat, stop swallowing it. Nobody's grading you.
quote: Let him be only a man for once; for neither philosophy nor empire takes away natural feeling.
author: Antoninus Pius
citation: Recorded in the Historia Augusta, Life of Antoninus Pius 10.5, trans. David Magie
caveat: The Historia Augusta is a late and sometimes unreliable source. Say 'recorded in the Historia Augusta', never 'Marcus wrote'.
tonight: Stop swallowing the thing in your throat.
broll: marble hall in low light
a young man alone turning away
rain on a stone step at dusk
candle burning low in a dark room

hook: Epictetus had one rule for the person you've stopped speaking to. It's about which end you pick it up by.
story: He said everything you're carrying has two handles. One you can lift. One you can't. If your brother's done you wrong and you pick the thing up by he wronged me, that handle breaks in your hand every time. You've probably proved that already.
lesson: So he says grab the other one: that he is your brother, that he was brought up with you. That's not forgiveness. That's choosing which end to hold so you can actually move it. If there's a message you've left sitting for weeks, the shame is why it's heavy, not the message. Send four words tonight. Been meaning to reply.
quote: Everything has two handles, the one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not.
author: Epictetus
citation: Enchiridion 43, trans. P. E. Matheson
tonight: Send four words: "Been meaning to reply."
broll: two hands lifting a heavy clay jar
an unanswered message on a phone
two brothers walking apart on a street
a doorway left open at night

hook: A Roman official admitted that when his daughter got sick, he ran out of the house. He couldn't watch.
story: He left. He stayed away until someone came and told him she was better. She recovered. And he was so ashamed of himself that he brought it to a philosopher. Epictetus didn't call him a coward. He asked one question: would you call it love if her mother had done it?
lesson: He hadn't loved her less. He'd run from the feeling instead of standing in it. That's the whole gap. Most of us aren't cold, we're overwhelmed, and then we're ashamed of leaving. If you walked out on something hard today, you're not a bad man. Go back in tomorrow. That's the entire repair.
quote: Convince me that you acted naturally, and I will convince you that everything which takes place according to nature takes place rightly.
author: Epictetus
citation: Discourses I.11, trans. George Long
caveat: Epictetus does argue the man was wrong. Do NOT include that beat - the script sails on 'he loved her, he was overwhelmed'.
tonight: Go back into the room you walked out of.
broll: empty hospital corridor at night
a father sitting in a parked car
a child's bedroom door ajar
dawn light through a kitchen window

hook: Epictetus gave his students a sentence to say out loud about their temper. It starts by assuming you lost it every single day.
story: He taught that a habit lives on whatever you feed it, so the cure isn't a vow, it's a count. And the count goes: I used to be in passion every day; now every second day; then every third, then every fourth. Reach thirty clear days, he said, and make an offering, because by then it's dying.
lesson: Look where he starts you. Not day one of a brand new man. Every day, then slightly less. He isn't asking you to stop losing your temper tonight, he's asking you to start counting. So the thing you said at four o'clock is day zero, not a relapse. Write today's date down.
quote: I used to be in passion every day; now every second day; then every third, then every fourth.
author: Epictetus
citation: Discourses II.18, trans. George Long
caveat: This is the sentence Epictetus HANDS THE STUDENT to say, not a diary entry. Say 'he wrote it for you to say' - never 'Epictetus confessed'.
tonight: Write today's date down. That's day one of the count.
broll: a hand marking a wall calendar
a man sitting on a kitchen floor at night
phone face down on a table
steam on a bathroom mirror

hook: The only thing Marcus Aurelius ever wrote was private, and he opened it with a list of what he owed other people. Nothing about himself.
story: Book one of the Meditations is just names and debts. His grandfather, for his temper. His mother, for the way she lived. His teachers, one by one. And then this entry: from Rusticus I received the impression that my character required improvement and discipline. He is thanking, by name, the man who told him he wasn't good enough yet.
lesson: The most powerful man alive, alone with a notebook, concluding that everything decent in him came from somebody else. You've got that list too. You're just not speaking to half of it. Tonight, name three people you owe. Then message the easiest one. No explanation, just: I was thinking about you.
quote: From Rusticus I received the impression that my character required improvement and discipline.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations 1.7, trans. George Long
tonight: Name three people you owe. Message the easiest one: "I was thinking about you."
broll: a hand writing a list in a notebook
a phone contacts screen at night
two men talking on a doorstep
old letters in a shoebox

hook: Marcus Aurelius left himself instructions for the morning after he'd failed again. The instruction is not try harder.
story: Book five. He tells himself not to be disgusted, nor discouraged, nor dissatisfied when he fails his own principles. When thou hast failed, return back again. Then the gentle part: don't come back to philosophy like a boy to a schoolmaster. Come back the way a man with sore eyes reaches for the sponge and the egg.
lesson: Not a punishment. A compress. He wrote it that way because he knew he'd be back again and again. So the streak you broke isn't a verdict on you. The returning is the practice. Tonight, take the smallest version of the thing you quit and do it once. Badly counts.
quote: When thou hast failed, return back again, and be content if the greater part of what thou doest is consistent with man's nature.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations 5.9, trans. George Long
caveat: Same book as the_note (Meditations 5.1) - do not schedule in the same week.
tonight: Do the smallest version of the thing you quit. Once. Badly.
broll: unused running shoes by a door
a man doing one push-up on a bedroom floor
a crossed-out habit tracker
kitchen light on late at night

hook: A man was lying awake over something that hadn't happened yet. Seneca sent him a rule for it that takes about four seconds to use.
story: Lucilius was braced for trouble that never arrived. Seneca broke it down: some things torment us more than they ought, some before they ought, and some when they ought not to torment us at all. What you run at midnight is nearly always the second one. Early.
lesson: Then the rule: weigh carefully your hopes as well as your fears, and whenever all the elements are in doubt, decide in your own favour. That isn't lying to yourself. It's refusing to hand a tied vote to the worst case. Take the thing you keep replaying and say: I don't know yet, so I'm deciding in my favour. Then put the phone down.
quote: Whenever all the elements are in doubt, decide in your own favour.
author: Seneca
citation: Moral Letters 13, trans. Richard M. Gummere
caveat: The channel already used 'we suffer more in imagination than in reality' (2026-06-30). Keep that line off the card - this runs on 13.13 instead.
tonight: Say: "I don't know yet, so I'm deciding in my favour."
broll: a man staring at a dark ceiling
phone screen at 1am, low brightness
an unopened envelope on a table
empty road seen from a bedroom window

hook: A young man went red in front of Seneca and was mortified about it. Seneca's verdict: no wisdom will ever fix that, so stop trying.
story: The kid had real ability, but the colour came up from somewhere deep and he knew the room had seen. Seneca wrote about him with unusual gentleness. Wisdom can never remove this habit, he said. It comes or goes unbidden, and is a law unto itself. What is inborn can be toned down, but not overcome.
lesson: Your body does what it does. The heat in your face, the hands, the voice going thin halfway through a sentence: none of it is character, and no discipline was ever going to delete it. The shame stacked on top is the only optional part. Put that down tonight. The blushing can stay.
quote: By no wisdom can natural weaknesses of the body be removed.
author: Seneca
citation: Moral Letters 11, trans. Richard M. Gummere
caveat: Never near unfinished (Letter 87) - both turn on Seneca and blushing.
tonight: Put down the shame. The blushing can stay.
broll: a man before a meeting in a stairwell
hands holding notes, shaking slightly
a face lit by a laptop screen
a man breathing out in a parked car

hook: Marcus Aurelius ran the Roman Empire, and kept writing himself notes about not wanting to get out of bed.
story: In his private notebook, this: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present. I am rising to the work of a human being. Read it again. He's arguing with himself. He even writes the other side's lines: but this is more pleasant. That's a man losing to his own blankets, in ink, as emperor.
lesson: Meditations isn't a book of answers. It's twenty years of the same man failing at the same small thing and writing the note again. He never fixed it. He just kept writing it. Tonight, write one line for tomorrow morning. One. Then sleep.
quote: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present: I am rising to the work of a human being.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations 5.1, trans. George Long
tonight: Write one line for tomorrow morning. Then sleep.
broll: unmade bed in grey morning light
a hand writing in a worn notebook
oil lamp on a desk before dawn
a man sitting on the edge of a bed

hook: Marcus Aurelius wrote down that he had failed at becoming a philosopher, while he was Emperor of Rome.
story: The opening of book eight. He tells himself it's obvious to everyone how far he is from the life he meant to live, and that he'll probably never be called a philosopher. Then, instead of a plan, he gives himself permission: stop caring how it looks, and live the rest of it the way your nature wants.
lesson: That's the Emperor of Rome writing off the version of himself he'd promised. He was nearly fifty. He did the job anyway for another ten years. If you're carrying a version of yourself you didn't become, you're allowed to put him down. Tonight, name him once, out loud. I'm not him.
quote: Be content then in the rest of thy life, and let nothing else distract thee.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations 8.1, trans. George Long
tonight: Say the name of the man you didn't become. Then say "I'm not him."
broll: a man looking at his reflection in a dark window
an old photograph face down
empty office at night
long road at dusk

hook: Seneca wrote the rulebook on how to grieve properly. Then his closest friend died and he did all of it wrong, and published that.
story: He'd written the advice. Don't be undone. Keep your feet. Then Annaeus Serenus died, younger than him, and Seneca fell apart. He put it in a letter, in public, under his own name. He said he wept so much that he must be counted among the examples of men who have been overcome by grief.
lesson: The most quoted man in Rome, filing himself in the failure column. He kept writing for years after. He was alright. If you didn't handle something the way you meant to, that doesn't cancel you. Tonight, say the name of whoever you lost. Just the name. That's allowed to be the whole thing.
quote: I wept so excessively for my dear friend that I must be included among the examples of men who have been overcome by grief.
author: Seneca
citation: Moral Letters 63.14, trans. Richard M. Gummere
caveat: Never schedule within two weeks of serenus_not_ill - same Serenus, and this reveals his death.
tonight: Say the name out loud. Just the name.
broll: empty chair by a window
rain on a dark street
a man alone at a table
candle going out

hook: The man who took over the Stoic school after Zeno was nicknamed "the Ass" by the other students. He kept the name on purpose.
story: Cleanthes was a boxer who came to Athens with four drachmas. To study under Zeno he hauled water in gardens all night, and he was so poor he wrote his notes on oyster shells. The other students called him the Ass. He kept it, and told them what it meant: he alone was strong enough to carry Zeno's load.
lesson: He wasn't the quick one. He was the one who kept turning up, and when Zeno died he got the school. If you're the slowest man in the room, that's a position, not a verdict. Name the thing you're bad at and say it out loud: I'm still carrying it.
quote: He did not mind being called the ass, telling them that he alone was strong enough to carry the load of Zeno.
author: Diogenes Laertius
citation: Lives of Eminent Philosophers VII.168, trans. R. D. Hicks
caveat: Compiled centuries later - say 'the story goes'. NEVER mention how Cleanthes died (he starved himself). Doctrine 5 violation; stays out of every version.
tonight: Name the thing you're bad at. Say: "I'm still carrying it."
broll: a man carrying water containers at night
empty gym at closing time
a tired man on a night bus
notes written on scrap paper

hook: Seneca got seasick on a short crossing, made the captain dump him on the rocks, then wrote it down and sent it to a friend.
story: A short hop across the bay of Naples. The water turned, and he went the kind of green that doesn't clear. His own account: I laid down the law to my pilot, forcing him to make for the shore, willy-nilly. The coast was rock. He went over the side in his cloak and scrambled in over the stones.
lesson: Then his real point. No man confesses what's wrong with him, he said, because he's still inside it. Saying it out loud is proof you're already surfacing. If you've been answering fine since about March, you don't need a plan tonight. You need one true sentence, said once, to one person.
quote: Therefore I laid down the law to my pilot, forcing him to make for the shore, willy-nilly.
author: Seneca
citation: Moral Letters 53, trans. Richard M. Gummere
caveat: Never within two weeks of first_hit or serenus_not_ill - three sea stories close together reads as a gimmick.
tonight: Say one true sentence to one person who knows you.
broll: a man leaning on a harbour railing
grey choppy water from a small boat
a phone with an unsent message at night
wet stones on a shoreline at dusk

hook: Seneca revisited his childhood home and complained the trees looked old. Then the old man at the door turned out to be his playmate.
story: He arrived in a mood: the stonework crumbling, the plane trees gnarled and bare. Then a worn-out old man at the door stood grinning at him, and Seneca asked who the decrepit man was. He said: I am Felicio. You used to bring me little images. My father was the steward here.
lesson: Everything he looked at that day was old, and then the mirror walked up and smiled. He didn't spiral. He wrote that no one is so old that it would be improper for him to hope for another day. If the years got away from you, tonight isn't the audit. Put one thing in tomorrow. One.
quote: No one is so old that it would be improper for him to hope for another day of existence.
author: Seneca
citation: Moral Letters 12, trans. Richard M. Gummere
caveat: Felicio was enslaved in Seneca's household. Do not sanitise him into 'an old friend' and do not stop to explain Roman slavery - say 'a man from the household' and keep moving.
tonight: Put one thing in tomorrow. One.
broll: an old front door with peeling paint
a man looking up at a bare tree
a childhood photograph in a drawer
empty kitchen in an old family house

hook: Marcus Aurelius wrote himself a warning that the job was turning him into someone he wouldn't like. He was the Emperor of Rome.
story: Book six, one line, to nobody but himself: take care that thou art not made into a Caesar, that thou art not dyed with this dye; for such things happen. Dyed. Like cloth in a vat: slowly, evenly, no moment where it happens. Then he lists what to hold on to. Simple. Good. Serious. Kind.
lesson: He could feel the job hardening him, and he wrote it down instead of pretending. If you've been getting shorter with people this year, colder than you were, that isn't your real character showing. That's the dye. Noticing is most of the defence. Name one person you've been sharp with. Tomorrow, be normal with them.
quote: Take care that thou art not made into a Caesar, that thou art not dyed with this dye.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations 6.30, trans. George Long
tonight: Name one person you've been sharp with. Tomorrow, be normal with them.
broll: ink spreading through water
a man's reflection in a dark office window
someone snapping a laptop shut
two people not speaking in a car

hook: A famous Stoic went white with fear in a storm at sea, and a rich passenger mocked him for it afterwards.
story: A Roman on that ship wrote it down. The philosopher didn't scream. But he went pale, and everyone saw. When the sea calmed, a wealthy Greek came over to needle him about it. The philosopher just pulled a book out of his bag, Epictetus, and showed him the passage.
lesson: The first hit lands on everyone. The body goes before the mind gets a vote. What makes you steady isn't never flinching. It's not agreeing with the flinch. So when your chest goes tight tonight for no reason, that's the first hit. It isn't cowardice. Put a hand flat on your chest and let it pass. It does.
quote: He is affected for a short time and slightly in his colour and expression, but does not assent.
author: Aulus Gellius
citation: Attic Nights 19.1, trans. John C. Rolfe
tonight: Hand flat on your chest. Let the first hit pass.
broll: storm waves against a ship hull
a man gripping a railing at sea
dark clouds over open water
calm sea after a storm

hook: Seneca put himself on trial every night before sleep, and wrote down the verdict he always handed himself.
story: He got it from his teacher Sextius, who asked himself at lights-out: what bad habit did you cure today? Seneca did the same. He replayed the day. Then this: I conceal nothing from myself, and omit nothing. Why should I be afraid of any of my shortcomings, when it is in my power to say, I pardon you this time, see that you never do that anymore?
lesson: He pardons himself. Every night. That's the part everyone leaves out. If you snapped at someone today and you've been chewing it since four o'clock, do the whole practice, not half. Look at it. Then say: pardoned. Not again. Sleep.
quote: I pardon you this time: see that you never do that anymore.
author: Seneca
citation: On Anger III.36, trans. Aubrey Stewart
tonight: Replay it once. Then say: "Pardoned. Not again."
broll: a man switching off a bedside lamp
hands washing a face in a dim bathroom
notebook closing
dark bedroom ceiling

hook: Seneca's prescription for a man who'd gone flat wasn't discipline or a cold bath. It was: go and be a bit ridiculous for an hour.
story: He wrote a book for a friend with no crisis, just nothing working. When he gets to the treatment, it isn't more effort. The mind must not be kept strained to the same pitch, he says; it ought sometimes to be relaxed by amusement. Socrates did not blush to play with little boys.
lesson: A Stoic, writing a prescription for messing about. He didn't think rest was the reward for finishing; he thought it was part of the machine, and the mind comes back keener for it. So the guilt you feel doing nothing tonight isn't information. Do one pointless thing you used to enjoy, twenty minutes. Don't earn it first.
quote: Neither ought we always to keep the mind strained to the same pitch, but it ought sometimes to be relaxed by amusement.
author: Seneca
citation: Of Peace of Mind XVII, trans. Aubrey Stewart
caveat: Same work as serenus_not_ill - not within two weeks. Seneca's next example is Cato relaxing with wine: CUT IT, the viewer may already be drinking more than he means to.
tonight: Twenty minutes of something pointless you used to like. Don't earn it first.
broll: a man playing a battered guitar at home
a football on grass at dusk
an old games console under a TV
a man walking a dog on a dark street

hook: Seneca was one of the richest men in Rome, and still went red in the face when a better-off group rode past him.
story: He was travelling rough on purpose, a farm cart, a mattress on the ground. Then a wealthier party rode by, and he felt his face go hot. He was in his sixties. He was the most famous philosopher alive. And he wrote it down: whenever we meet a more sumptuous party I blush in spite of myself.
lesson: Then he named what it was. Not a sin, just proof that the thing he believed hadn't fully moved in yet. That's all it is when you feel behind your friends. Not weakness. Unfinished. Tonight, when you catch yourself measuring, say the word unfinished, out loud if you can. Then let it go.
quote: Whenever we meet a more sumptuous party I blush in spite of myself.
author: Seneca
citation: Moral Letters 87.4, trans. Richard M. Gummere
tonight: When you catch yourself comparing, say one word: "unfinished."
broll: a slow cart on a country road
expensive cars passing at night
a man watching from a roadside
dust settling on a track

hook: Someone told Seneca he had no right to give anyone advice, given the state of his own life. Seneca agreed with him.
story: Lucilius called him out: you're telling me how to live and you haven't sorted yourself. Seneca didn't argue. He wrote: I am not so shameless as to undertake to cure my fellow-men when I am ill myself. And then, he's sharing the remedy just as if we were lying ill in the same hospital.
lesson: Same hospital. Not doctor and patient. Two men in the ward. If you've been quietly disqualifying yourself from helping your mate, from starting again, from calling anyone, because you're not fixed yet, that rule is invented. Nobody's fixed. Tonight, say the thing you'd say to a friend, to yourself, in his voice.
quote: I am sharing the remedy with you, just as if we were lying ill in the same hospital.
author: Seneca
citation: Moral Letters 27.1, trans. Richard M. Gummere
tonight: Say to yourself, in the voice you'd use on a friend, the thing you'd tell him.
broll: two beds in a dim room
a man writing a letter by lamplight
hospital window at night
two chairs facing each other

hook: The founder of Stoicism couldn't handle crowds. At dinner he sat at the end of the couch so only one person could get near him.
story: Diogenes Laertius collected the small stuff: sour-faced, awkward in company, avoided a crowd with great care. Then this. He disliked to be brought too near to people, so that he would take the end seat of a couch, saving himself from one half of the inconvenience. He still went. He just sat where one man could reach him.
lesson: The man who founded the whole philosophy of endurance found a room full of people exhausting. Being drained by company isn't coldness and it isn't a defect. So don't cancel Saturday. Go, take the seat at the end, and let yourself leave at ten. Turning up tired still counts.
quote: He disliked, they say, to be brought too near to people, so that he would take the end seat of a couch.
author: Diogenes Laertius
citation: Lives of Eminent Philosophers VII.14, trans. R. D. Hicks
caveat: Gossip a compiler wrote down centuries later - say 'the story goes'. Never diagnose Zeno with anything modern.
tonight: Don't cancel. Go, take the seat at the end, leave at ten.
broll: a man alone at the edge of a busy bar
a full dinner table seen from the end
a coat by a front door at night
a man sitting in a car outside a house

hook: Marcus Aurelius had to talk himself into being around people before he got out of bed. He wrote the script down so it was ready.
story: Book two opens with it. Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. He isn't being bitter, he's bracing. He names them in advance so that when one turns up at nine it's a forecast, not an ambush. Then: I can't hate them, we're built to work together.
lesson: The Emperor of Rome needed a run-up to Monday morning. So the dread about tomorrow's room isn't softness, and here's the workaround: have the meeting now, in your head, where it's cheap. Say out loud who is going to be hard work tomorrow. Naming them takes the charge out.
quote: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations 2.1, trans. George Long
tonight: Say out loud who's going to be hard work tomorrow.
broll: alarm clock glowing at 5am
a man sitting on the edge of a bed
office lift doors opening
commuters on a platform in the dark

hook: Seneca wrote the most quoted line there is about wasting time, and in the same letter admitted he was still wasting his.
story: Letter one. He tells Lucilius that while we are postponing, life speeds by. Then he opens his own books: I cannot boast that I waste nothing, but I can at least tell you what I am wasting. I can give you the reasons why I am a poor man.
lesson: He never claimed to have fixed it. He claimed to know where the leak was, which is a smaller ask than becoming a disciplined man, and it's the only part that ever works. So don't build a system tonight. Name the one hour you lose every day and where it goes. You're allowed to lose it again tomorrow.
quote: While we are postponing, life speeds by.
author: Seneca
citation: Moral Letters 1, trans. Richard M. Gummere
caveat: Absolution first. If something must be cut for time, cut the hook, never the 'poor man' confession - without it this becomes a lecture.
tonight: Name the one hour you lose every day and where it goes.
broll: a man scrolling in bed in the dark
clock hands moving on a wall
an empty desk with a cold coffee
streetlights through a window at 1am

hook: Epictetus told beginners the actual price of getting good at anything: for a while, you have to be willing to look stupid.
story: Rule thirteen of his handbook is blunt. If you would improve, submit to be considered without sense and foolish. Wish to be considered to know nothing. And if people start treating you as important, he says, distrust yourself. He's talking to men at the start of something, in a room of people already good at it.
lesson: Nobody skips the stretch where they're the worst one there. What makes men quit isn't difficulty, it's being watched while they're bad. He says out loud that looking stupid is the entrance fee, not proof you don't belong. Tonight, book the thing you're bad at. Be the worst man in the room on Thursday.
quote: If you would improve, submit to be considered without sense and foolish.
author: Epictetus
citation: Enchiridion 13, trans. George Long
caveat: Long's wording is archaic - read it as written, never paraphrase into a modern-sounding 'quote'. Other translations say 'foolish and stupid'; that is NOT Long and must not carry his name.
tonight: Book the thing you're bad at. Be the worst one there on Thursday.
broll: a beginner in the corner of a gym
a man watching a class from the doorway
hands fumbling with new equipment
an empty studio with the lights on

hook: A Roman senator was being tried in his absence. When the news reached him, he checked the time and went to take his exercise.
story: Agrippinus wasn't in the room and couldn't affect it. Word came: the Senate was hearing his case. He said he hoped it went well, noticed it was the fifth hour, his time for exercise and a cold bath, and went. He came back, and they told him: condemned to banishment. He said: let us go to Aricia then, and dine.
lesson: That isn't nerve. It's a rule made in advance for what he does while others decide. If you're waiting on a reply that isn't coming until Monday, the waiting doesn't move it and it costs you the evening. Do the ordinary next thing on your list. Then eat.
quote: Let us go to Aricia then, and dine.
author: Agrippinus, quoted by Epictetus
citation: Discourses I.1, trans. George Long
caveat: End the script at dinner. Nothing about his end, and never frame the exile itself as the inspiring part.
tonight: Do the ordinary next thing on your list. Then eat.
broll: a man tying running shoes in a hallway
clock on a kitchen wall
phone lighting up on a desk, ignored
a plate of food under a kitchen light

hook: A philosopher walked into an advancing army to talk them out of the war. They laughed at him until he gave up and walked away.
story: Rome, sixty-nine AD. Musonius Rufus joined a peace delegation, walked in among armed soldiers, and argued the blessings of peace and the perils of war. Tacitus records it: many thought it ridiculous, more thought it tiresome, and some were ready to knock him down, so he stopped. He walked away having achieved nothing, in front of everyone.
lesson: Then he went home and kept teaching, and one of the young men in his room became Epictetus. Everything you know from Epictetus came through a man who'd been laughed out of a field. The worst thing you did in front of people is not the last thing about you.
quote: Many thought it ridiculous, more thought it tiresome.
author: Tacitus
citation: Histories III.81, trans. Church and Brodribb
tonight: Name the humiliation once, in the past tense.
broll: a lone figure facing a crowd
dust on a roman road
a man walking away across a field
a teacher with students in a small room

hook: Zeno lost an entire ship's cargo at thirty and washed up broke in a strange city. What he did that afternoon started Stoicism.
story: He was a merchant, not a philosopher. Purple dye, a full ship, gone. He came up into Athens, wandered into a bookseller's shop and started reading. It was Xenophon, about Socrates. He looked up and asked the bookseller where he could find men like that. The bookseller pointed at a man walking past and said, follow him. He did.
lesson: Later he said: I made a prosperous voyage when I suffered shipwreck. Not a lesson, just what happened. Losing the thing isn't always the end of the story. Sometimes it's the part before it. Tonight, one thing you lost this year. Ask what it made room for. Don't force an answer.
quote: I made a prosperous voyage when I suffered shipwreck.
author: Zeno of Citium
citation: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII.4, trans. R. D. Hicks
caveat: Diogenes Laertius gives two versions. Say 'the story goes', not 'we know'.
tonight: Name one thing you lost this year. Ask what it made room for.
broll: wrecked cargo on a shore
an old bookshop interior
a man reading alone
harbour at first light

hook: Seneca spent a whole letter proving a strong mind can work through unbearable noise. The last line is him admitting he moved out.
story: He was living above a public bath. He lists all of it: men grunting under weights, the slap of a massage, the drinks seller shouting, and the man whose armpits are being plucked, screaming. Then he argues, brilliantly, that a settled mind doesn't need quiet. And at the end he just says: why should I torment myself any longer, when the fix is this easy?
lesson: He wanted to test himself. He'd tested himself. He left. You don't get points for enduring something you're allowed to change. Tonight, pick the one thing you've been white-knuckling that has an actual door. Don't solve it. Just admit out loud that the door exists.
quote: Why need I be tormented any longer?
author: Seneca
citation: Moral Letters 56.15, trans. Richard M. Gummere
tonight: Name the thing you've been enduring that has a door.
broll: noisy street seen from a window
a man packing a single bag
an open door in a dark hallway
quiet room at last

hook: Someone stole Epictetus's lamp in the night. His reaction has irritated people for two thousand years.
story: He kept an iron lamp beside his household gods. One night he heard a noise at the window, ran down, and it was gone. He didn't rage. He said the reason he lost the lamp was that the thief was better than him at staying awake, and that the thief paid for it by becoming a thief. Tomorrow, he said, buy an earthenware one.
lesson: That's it. No lesson about the universe. He was better at staying up, I'll get a cheaper lamp. Most of what's eating you tonight is lamp-sized. Pick one thing you're still angry about that cost under fifty bucks. Say earthenware, and drop it.
quote: The reason why I lost my lamp was that the thief was superior to me in vigilance.
author: Epictetus
citation: Discourses I.29.21, trans. George Long
tonight: Pick one grudge that cost under fifty bucks. Say "earthenware."
broll: an old oil lamp burning
an empty shelf at night
a shuttered window
a plain clay lamp on a table
